claim: Rbfox2 is expressed in neural crest cells (NCCs) during mouse embryogenesis.
source: Here, we demonstrate that splicing factor Rbfox2 is expressed in the neural crest cells (NCCs), and deletion of Rbfox2 in NCCs leads to cleft palate and defects in craniofacial bone development.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data showing Rbfox2 expression in NCCs at E9.5-E11.5 (Figure 1) and text description of expression pattern.

claim: Deletion of Rbfox2 in NCCs leads to cleft palate.
source: Here, we demonstrate that splicing factor Rbfox2 is expressed in the neural crest cells (NCCs), and deletion of Rbfox2 in NCCs leads to cleft palate and defects in craniofacial bone development.
evidence: Supported by morphological and histological data showing cleft palate in Rbfox2Pax3-CKO and Rbfox2Wnt1-CKO embryos (Figure 2).

claim: Deletion of Rbfox2 in NCCs leads to defects in craniofacial bone development.
source: Here, we demonstrate that splicing factor Rbfox2 is expressed in the neural crest cells (NCCs), and deletion of Rbfox2 in NCCs leads to cleft palate and defects in craniofacial bone development.
evidence: Supported by skeletal staining data showing hypoplastic and malformed craniofacial bones in Rbfox2 mutants (Figure 4).

claim: Rbfox2 regulates splicing and expression of numerous genes essential for neural crest/craniofacial development.
source: RNA-Seq analysis revealed that Rbfox2 regulates splicing and expression of numerous genes essential for neural crest/craniofacial development.
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data identifying 81 differentially expressed transcripts and 56 differentially expressed genes (Figure 5).

claim: Rbfox2-TGF-β-Tak1 signaling axis is deregulated by Rbfox2 deletion.
source: We demonstrate that Rbfox2-TGF-β-Tak1 signaling axis is deregulated by Rbfox2 deletion.
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing reduced Tak1, pTak1, pSmad2-C, and p-p38 Mapk levels in Rbfox2 mutants (Figure 6A, D).

claim: Restoration of TGF-β signaling by Tak1 overexpression can rescue the proliferation defect seen in Rbfox2 mutants.
source: Furthermore, restoration of TGF-β signaling by Tak1 overexpression can rescue the proliferation defect seen in Rbfox2 mutants.
evidence: Supported by Ki67 immunostaining data showing increased proliferation in Rbfox2 mutant cells after Tak1 overexpression (Figure 6F-H).

claim: TGF-β signaling promotes expression of Rbfox2 in NCCs through a positive feedback loop.
source: We also identified a positive feedback loop in which TGF-β signaling promotes expression of Rbfox2 in NCCs.
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing increased Rbfox2 expression after TGF-β stimulation (Figure 7A) and luciferase assays showing Smad-dependent activation of Rbfox2 promoter (Figure 7E-G).

claim: At E9.5, Rbfox2 is expressed in the premigratory NCCs at the dorsal neural tube, as well as in the migratory NCCs throughout the rostrocaudal axis.
source: At E9.5, Rbfox2 is expressed in the premigratory NCCs at the dorsal neural tube, as well as in the migratory NCCs (Figure 1A–C,F–H,K–M) throughout the rostrocaudal axis, with strong expression of Rbfox2 observed in the somites.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining images showing Rbfox2 expression pattern at E9.5 (Figure 1A-C, F-H, K-M).

claim: Rbfox2 expression is observed with strong expression in the somites at E9.5.
source: At E9.5, Rbfox2 is expressed in the premigratory NCCs at the dorsal neural tube, as well as in the migratory NCCs (Figure 1A–C,F–H,K–M) throughout the rostrocaudal axis, with strong expression of Rbfox2 observed in the somites.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining images showing Rbfox2 expression in somites (Figure 1).

claim: Rbfox2 expression is gradually reduced in migratory NCCs.
source: Rbfox2 expression is gradually reduced in migratory NCCs (Figure 1K–M).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining images showing reduced Rbfox2 expression in migratory NCCs (Figure 1K-M).

claim: Rbfox2 expression was detected in the neural crest-derived craniofacial tissues including the palate shelves.
source: Rbfox2 expression was detected in the neural crest-derived craniofacial tissues including the palate shelves but not in the cardiac tissues such as OFT (Figure 1D–E,I–J,N–O).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining images showing Rbfox2 expression in palate shelves (Figure 1D-E, I-J, N-O).

claim: Rbfox2 expression was not detected in the cardiac tissues such as OFT.
source: Rbfox2 expression was detected in the neural crest-derived craniofacial tissues including the palate shelves but not in the cardiac tissues such as OFT (Figure 1D–E,I–J,N–O).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining images showing absence of Rbfox2 expression in OFT (Figure 1D-E, I-J, N-O).

claim: At E9.5, Rbfox2 expression is identical to Pax3 in NCCs, dorsal neural tube, and somites.
source: At E9.5, Rbfox2 expression is identical to Pax3 in NCCs, dorsal neural tube, and somites (Figure 1P and S).
evidence: Supported by comparative immunostaining images of Rbfox2 and Pax3 at E9.5 (Figure 1P, S).

claim: At E10.5, in addition to premigratory NCCs, Rbfox2 is also expressed in the dorsal root ganglia.
source: At E10.5, in addition to premigratory NCCs, Rbfox2 is also expressed in the dorsal root ganglia (Figure 1Q).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining images showing Rbfox2 expression in dorsal root ganglia at E10.5 (Figure 1Q).

claim: At E10.5, in contrast to Pax3 expression in the dorsal neural tube, the Rbfox2 expression is more restricted to the ventral neural tube.
source: In contrast to Pax3 expression in the dorsal neural tube, the Rbfox2 expression is more restricted to the ventral neural tube (Figure 1Q and T).
evidence: Supported by comparative immunostaining images showing different expression patterns of Rbfox2 and Pax3 in neural tube at E10.5 (Figure 1Q, T).

claim: At E11.5, Rbfox2 is expressed in the ventral neural tube and dorsal root ganglia.
source: At E11.5, Rbfox2 is expressed in the ventral neural tube and dorsal root ganglia (Figure 1R).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining images showing Rbfox2 expression pattern at E11.5 (Figure 1R).

claim: At E11.5, Pax3 is more restricted to the dorsal neural tube.
source: However, Pax3 is more restricted to the dorsal neural tube (Figure 1U).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining images showing Pax3 expression pattern at E11.5 (Figure 1U).

claim: Pax3Cre/+-mediated deletion of Rbfox2 results in neonatal lethality.
source: We observed that Pax3Cre/+-mediated deletion of Rbfox2 results in neonatal lethality.
evidence: Supported by genotyping data showing no mutant pups recovered at postnatal day 10 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Rbfox2Pax3-CKO embryos develop a cleft palate and defects in the development of craniofacial skeleton.
source: Rbfox2 mutant (Rbfox2Pax3-CKO) embryos develop a cleft palate and defects in the development of craniofacial skeleton, suggesting defective cranial neural crest development.
evidence: Supported by morphological and histological data showing cleft palate and craniofacial defects (Figure 2, Figure 4).

claim: Rbfox2Wnt1-CKO mutants developed a cleft palate and craniofacial skeleton defects and died postnatally at day 1.
source: Similar to Rbfox2Pax3-CKO embryos, Rbfox2Wnt1-CKO mutants developed a cleft palate and craniofacial skeleton defects and died postnatally at day 1.
evidence: Supported by morphological and histological data showing cleft palate and craniofacial defects in Rbfox2Wnt1-CKO embryos (Figure 2M-T, Figure 4L-S).

claim: Rbfox2Pax3-CKO embryos are present at the expected Mendelian ratios at all embryonic time points analyzed (E10.5-E18.5).
source: Genotyping of embryos from series of timed point matings demonstrated that Rbfox2Pax3-CKO embryos are present at the expected Mendelian ratios at all embryonic time points analyzed (E10.5-E18.5) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by genotyping data showing expected Mendelian ratios at embryonic stages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Rbfox2Pax3-CKO mutant pups die at postnatal day one (P1).
source: However, pups monitoring after birth revealed that mutant pups that are characterized by a shortened body axis and abnormal craniofacial features die at postnatal day one (P1) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and G).
evidence: Supported by genotyping data showing no mutant pups at P10 and morphological data at P1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B, G).

claim: Rbfox2Pax3-CKO embryos develop severe subcutaneous edema in mid- and late-gestation.
source: Our morphological and histological analyses demonstrate that Rbfox2Pax3-CKO embryos develop cleft palate and severe subcutaneous edema, which are present in mid- and late-gestation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–F,H–K).
evidence: Supported by morphological and histological images showing edema in Rbfox2Pax3-CKO embryos (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-F, H-K).

claim: The neonatal lethality in Rbfox2Pax3-CKO pups is caused by respiratory failure.
source: Irregular breathing and hardly inflated lungs in Rbfox2Pax3-CKO pups support the notion that the neonatal lethality is caused by respiratory failure (Figure 2—figure supplement 1L–O).
evidence: Supported by histological images showing uninflated lungs in Rbfox2Pax3-CKO pups (Figure 2—figure supplement 1L-O).

claim: In Rbfox2Pax3-CKO embryos, development of primary palates is not affected.
source: In Rbfox2Pax3-CKO embryos, development of primary palates is not affected.
evidence: Stated in text without specific figure reference, but consistent with focus on secondary palate defects.

claim: All of the Rbfox2Pax3-CKO pups died neonatally, exhibiting a secondary cleft palate defect.
source: However, all of the Rbfox2Pax3-CKO pups died neonatally, exhibiting a secondary cleft palate defect.
evidence: Supported by genotyping data showing no mutant pups at P10 and morphological data showing cleft palate (Figure 2).

claim: At E12.5, the palatal shelves in both control and Rbfox2Pax3-CKO embryos were initiated normally, growing vertically flanking the developing tongue.
source: At E12.5, the palatal shelves in both control and Rbfox2Pax3-CKO embryos were initiated normally, growing vertically flanking the developing tongue (Figure 2A–B,G–H).
evidence: Supported by morphological and histological images showing normal palatal shelf orientation at E12.5 (Figure 2A-B, G-H).

claim: No obvious morphological or histological differences were observed between control and Rbfox2Pax3-CKO embryos at E12.5.
source: No obvious morphological or histological differences were observed at this embryonic stage.
evidence: Stated in text describing E12.5 palatal shelves, supported by Figure 2A-B, G-H.

claim: At E15.5 and E18.5, the control palatal shelves were elevated above the tongue to a horizontal position and met each other at the midline along the anterior-posterior axis.
source: At E15.5 and E18.5, the control palatal shelves were elevated above the tongue to a horizontal position and met each other at the midline along the anterior-posterior axis (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: Supported by morphological and histological images showing normal palate fusion in controls (Figure 2C-F).

claim: In Rbfox2Pax3-CKO embryos, palatal shelves were elevated above the tongue to a horizontal position, but they completely failed to fuse at the midline throughout the anterior-posterior axis.
source: However, in Rbfox2Pax3-CKO embryos, palatal shelves were elevated above the tongue to a horizontal position, but they completely failed to fuse at the midline throughout the anterior-posterior axis (Figure 2I–L).
evidence: Supported by morphological and histological images showing cleft palate in Rbfox2Pax3-CKO embryos (Figure 2I-L).

claim: Rbfox2Wnt1-CKO mice were born at the expected Mendelian ratio but died at P1.
source: Similar to Rbfox2Pax3-CKO, Rbfox2Wnt1-CKO mice were born at the expected Mendelian ratio but died at P1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1P–R).
evidence: Supported by genotyping data showing expected Mendelian ratios at embryonic stages but no mutants at P10 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1P).

claim: In Rbfox2Wnt1-CKO embryos, palatal shelves were elevated above the tongue to a horizontal position, but completely failed to fuse at the midline throughout the anterior-posterior axis.
source: Similar to Rbfox2Pax3-CKO embryos, palatal shelves in Rbfox2Wnt1-CKO embryos were elevated above the tongue to a horizontal position, but completely failed to fuse at the midline throughout the anterior-posterior axis (Figure 2M–T).
evidence: Supported by morphological and histological images showing cleft palate in Rbfox2Wnt1-CKO embryos (Figure 2M-T).

claim: Ki67 immunohistochemistry revealed a significant reduction in cell proliferation in Rbfox2 mutants when compared with control embryos at E12.5.
source: Ki67 immunohistochemistry revealed a significant reduction in cell proliferation in Rbfox2 mutants when compared with control embryos at E12.5, in which the morphological or histological changes were not evident (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Supported by Ki67 immunostaining and quantification showing reduced proliferation at E12.5 (Figure 3A-C).

claim: A significant difference in cell proliferation was more evident at E15.5 in Rbfox2 mutants compared to controls.
source: A significant difference in cell proliferation was more evident at E15.5 (Figure 3D–F and G–I).
evidence: Supported by Ki67 immunostaining and quantification showing reduced proliferation at E15.5 (Figure 3D-F, G-I).

claim: TUNEL assay demonstrated no differences in cell death between the control and Rbfox2 mutants at E15.5.
source: TUNEL assay demonstrated no differences in cell death between the control and Rbfox2 mutants at E15.5 (Figure 3J–K).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay images showing similar apoptosis levels (Figure 3J-K).

claim: E-cadherin expression is observed in the nasal, palatal and tongue epithelium and not affected by Rbfox2 deletion.
source: E-cadherin expression is observed in the nasal, palatal and tongue epithelium and not affected by Rbfox2 deletion (Figure 3L–M).
evidence: Supported by E-cadherin immunostaining images showing similar expression patterns in control and mutant (Figure 3L-M).

claim: Labeled neural crest cells marked by GFP immunostaining were abundantly present in the palate shelves of mutant embryos at E15.5.
source: Labeled neural crest cells marked by GFP immunostaining were abundantly present in the palate shelves of mutant embryos (Figure 3N–O).
evidence: Supported by GFP immunostaining images showing neural crest-derived cells in mutant palate shelves (Figure 3N-O).

claim: No obvious NCCs migration defect was observed in Rbfox2 mutant embryos at E12.5 and E14.5.
source: No obvious NCCs migration defect was observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by lineage-tracing images showing similar NCC distribution in control and mutant embryos (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: In both Rbfox2Pax3-CKO and Rbfox2Wnt1-CKO embryos, neural crest-derived frontal bones of the calvaria were hypoplastic and widely separated leaving a wide dorsal opening.
source: In both Rbfox2Pax3-CKO and Rbfox2Wnt1-CKO embryos, neural crest-derived bones such as frontal bones of the calvaria were hypoplastic and widely separated leaving a wide dorsal opening (Figure 4C and M).
evidence: Supported by skeletal staining images showing hypoplastic frontal bones (Figure 4C, M).

claim: Decreased ossification of nasal bone was observed in Rbfox2Pax3-CKO mutant embryos compared to the controls.
source: Decreased ossification of nasal bone was observed in Rbfox2Pax3-CKO mutant embryos compared to the controls (Figure 4B–C and L–M).
evidence: Supported by skeletal staining images showing reduced nasal bone ossification (Figure 4B-C, L-M).

claim: Reduction in the lower jaw or mandible size was observed in Rbfox2 mutant embryos.
source: Reduction in the lower jaw or mandible size was observed in Rbfox2 mutant embryos (Figure 4E–H and N–Q).
evidence: Supported by skeletal staining images showing smaller mandible (Figure 4E-H, N-Q).

claim: Both the shape and size of most neural crest-derived bones including alisphenoid, premaxilla, palatal process of premaxilla, palatal process of maxilla and palatine are affected in Rbfox2 mutant embryos.
source: Further analysis revealed that both the shape and size of most neural crest-derived bones including alisphenoid, premaxilla, palatal process of premaxilla, palatal process of maxilla and palatine are affected in Rbfox2 mutant embryos (Figure 4J–K and R–S).
evidence: Supported by skeletal staining images showing malformed craniofacial bones (Figure 4J-K, R-S).

claim: The palatal process of palatine bone is missing in Rbfox2 mutant embryos.
source: The palatal process of palatine bone is also missing in Rbfox2 mutant embryos (Figure 4K and S).
evidence: Supported by skeletal staining images showing absence of palatal process of palatine bone (Figure 4K, S).

claim: Ectopic bone formation and fusion of vertebral bodies were observed in Rbfox2Pax3-CKO embryos.
source: Ectopic bone formation and fusion of vertebral bodies were observed in Rbfox2Pax3-CKO embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by skeletal staining images showing vertebral defects (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).

claim: No defects in the axial skeletons were observed in Rbfox2Wnt1-CKO embryos.
source: No defects in the axial skeletons were observed in Rbfox2Wnt1-CKO embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by skeletal staining images showing normal axial skeleton in Rbfox2Wnt1-CKO embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Reduced thickness in the ossified calvaria bone was observed in Rbfox2Pax3-CKO embryos.
source: Von Kossa staining of the calvaria from E17.5 Rbfox2Pax3-CKO mutant embryos revealed the impaired development of mesenchymal condensations that become ossified bone (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C). Reduced thickness in the ossified calvaria bone was observed in Rbfox2Pax3-CKO embryos.
evidence: Supported by Von Kossa staining images showing reduced bone thickness (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).

claim: The development of cardiac OFT was not affected in Rbfox2 mutants.
source: As shown by normal septation and alignment of the aorta and pulmonary trunk, the development of cardiac OFT was not affected in Rbfox2 mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–J).
evidence: Supported by morphological and histological images showing normal OFT development (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-J).

claim: Cardiac NCCs migration was grossly intact in the Rbfox2 mutant embryos.
source: Fate-mapping analysis demonstrated that cardiac NCCs migration was grossly intact in the Rbfox2 mutant embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 2K–P).
evidence: Supported by fate-mapping images showing normal cardiac NCC distribution (Figure 4—figure supplement 2K-P).

claim: The neurofilament 2H3 staining in Rbfox2 mutant embryos revealed abnormalities in the oculomotor (III), trochlear (IV) and hypoglossal nerve (XII cranial nerve).
source: The neurofilament 2H3 staining in Rbfox2 mutant embryos revealed abnormalities in the oculomotor (III), trochlear (IV) and hypoglossal nerve (XII cranial nerve) (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by whole mount neurofilament staining images showing cranial nerve defects (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).

claim: Oculomotor and trochlear nerves appear to be deformed in Rbfox2Pax3-CKO embryos.
source: Oculomotor and trochlear nerves appear to be deformed.
evidence: Stated in text describing cranial nerve analysis, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The hypoglossal cranial nerve is disorganized and shorter in Rbfox2Pax3-CKO embryos.
source: The hypoglossal cranial nerve is disorganized and shorter in Rbfox2Pax3-CKO embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by whole mount neurofilament staining images showing hypoglossal nerve defects (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).

claim: No significant difference was observed in the size of the dorsal root ganglion between control and Rbfox2Pax3-CKO embryos.
source: No significant difference was observed in the size of the dorsal root ganglion (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by quantification of dorsal root ganglia size (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).

claim: Enteric nervous system development was not affected in the absence of Rbfox2.
source: Enteric nervous system development was not affected in the absence of Rbfox2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C–D).
evidence: Supported by whole mount neurofilament staining and lineage tracing images showing normal enteric nervous system (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C-D).

claim: Thymus was not affected in Rbfox2 mutant embryos.
source: Similarly, other neural crest-derived organs such as thymus and adrenal gland (chromaffin cells) were not affected in Rbfox2 mutant embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 4, and Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by morphological and histological images showing normal thymus development (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).

claim: Adrenal gland (chromaffin cells) was not affected in Rbfox2 mutant embryos.
source: Similarly, other neural crest-derived organs such as thymus and adrenal gland (chromaffin cells) were not affected in Rbfox2 mutant embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 4, and Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by morphological, histological, and immunostaining images showing normal adrenal gland development (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).

claim: No significant changes were found in limb and diaphragm muscles in Rbfox2Pax3-CKO embryos.
source: Since Pax3Cre/+ transgene is active in non-neural crest-derived tissues such as limb and diaphragm muscles, we also analyzed these tissues and found no significant changes (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by histological images showing normal muscle development (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).

claim: Using MISO analysis, 81 differentially expressed transcripts from 59 genes were identified in Rbfox2 mutant samples as compared with control.
source: Using MISO analysis, we identified 81 differentially expressed transcripts from 59 genes in Rbfox2 mutant samples as compared with control (Figure 5B and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data analysis using MISO (Figure 5B).

claim: Cuffdiff analysis identified 33 alternatively spliced transcripts from 30 genes in Rbfox2 mutant samples as compared with controls.
source: However, Cuffdiff analysis identified 33 alternatively spliced transcripts from 30 genes in Rbfox2 mutant samples as compared with controls (Figure 5C and Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data analysis using Cuffdiff (Figure 5C).

claim: Pathway enrichment analysis identified significant enrichment of genes that control cellular and anatomical structure morphogenesis.
source: Pathway enrichment analysis identified significant enrichment of genes that control cellular and anatomical structure morphogenesis (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis of RNA-Seq data (Figure 5D).

claim: Significant UGCAUG motif enrichment was identified only in the introns of the Rbfox2 target genes (adjusted p-value=1.4E-08).
source: We performed an analysis of motif enrichment (AME) through the MEME suite (version 5.0.5) and identified significant UGCAUG motif enrichment only in the introns of the Rbfox2 target genes (adjusted p-value=1.4E-08) (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis of RNA-Seq data (Figure 5E).

claim: Most UGCAUG sequences were located within 1000 bases of the exon on either flanking introns in Rbfox2 target genes.
source: Most UGCAUG sequences were located within 1000 bases of the exon on either flanking introns (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by FIMO analysis showing location of UGCAUG sequences (Figure 5F).

claim: Venn analysis identified 11 transcripts that were identified by both MISO and Cuffdiff programs.
source: Venn analysis identified 11 transcripts that were identified by both programs and constituted a high confidence set of differentially expressed and AS isoforms in Rbfox2 mutants (Figure 5G–H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Venn diagram analysis of RNA-Seq data (Figure 5G-H).

claim: Rbfox2 deletion significantly impacted splicing and expression of Map3k7, Fn1, Postn and Uap1.
source: Using RNA isolated from control and Rbfox2 knockout craniofacial tissues, we validated the splicing changes identified by RNA-Seq by performing reverse transcriptase PCR (RT-PCR) in a selected group of genes such as mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase kinase 7 (Map3k7), fibronectin 1 (Fn1), periostin (Postn) and UAP1 UDP-N-acetylglucosamine pyrophosphorylase 1 (Uap1). Rbfox2 deletion significantly impacted splicing and expression of these candidate genes (Figure 5I–L).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR validation and qRT-PCR data (Figure 5I-L).

claim: Rbfox2 deletion reduced the expression of the predominantly expressed Map3k7 transcript.
source: For example, Rbfox2 deletion reduced the expression of the predominantly expressed Map3k7 transcript.
evidence: Stated in text describing RT-PCR validation results, supported by Figure 5I, L.

claim: The short Fn1 transcript was not present in Rbfox2 mutants.
source: The short Fn1 transcript was not present in Rbfox2 mutants.
evidence: Stated in text describing RT-PCR validation results, supported by Figure 5I.

claim: Rbfox2 can directly bind to the RNA of Map3k7, Fn1, Postn and Uap1 target genes and modulate splicing.
source: To determine that Rbfox2 directly bind to these target genes in vivo, we performed RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP) assays using anti-Rbfox2 antibody on palatal mesenchymal cells, followed by quantitative RT-PCR. We observed significant enrichment suggesting that Rbfox2 can directly bind to the RNA of these target genes and modulate splicing (Figure 5J).
evidence: Supported by RNA-IP assay data showing enrichment of target transcripts (Figure 5J).

claim: 56 differentially expressed genes were identified between control and Rbfox2 knockouts.
source: To determine the transcriptional changes associated with the craniofacial defects, we analyzed genes that are differentially expressed between control and Rbfox2 knockouts. We identified 56 differentially expressed genes (Figure 5K).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data analysis showing differentially expressed genes (Figure 5K).

claim: A significant reduction in Map3k7, Fn1, Myl1, Sfrs18 and Smarca2 was observed in Rbfox2 knockout tissues.
source: We observed a significant reduction in Map3k7, Fn1, Myl1, Sfrs18 and Smarca2 in Rbfox2 knockout tissues (Figure 5L).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR validation data (Figure 5L).

claim: Both Tak1 and phosphorylated Tak1 levels were significantly reduced in Rbfox2 mutant embryos.
source: To identify if TGF-β signaling pathway is affected by Rbfox2 deletion in vivo, we harvested palatal shelves from control and Rbfox2 mutant embryos and performed western blot analysis for Tak1 and phosphorylated Tak1. We found that both Tak1 and phosphorylated Tak1 levels were significantly reduced in Rbfox2 mutant embryos, demonstrating impaired TGF-β signaling pathway in neural crest-derived palate shelves (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing reduced Tak1 and pTak1 levels (Figure 6A).

claim: The level of C-terminal Smad2 phosphorylation was significantly reduced in Rbfox2 mutant embryos.
source: The level of C-terminal Smad2 phosphorylation was significantly reduced; however, no change in total Smad2 was observed.
evidence: Stated in text describing western blot results, supported by Figure 6A.

claim: No change in total Smad2 was observed in Rbfox2 mutant embryos.
source: The level of C-terminal Smad2 phosphorylation was significantly reduced; however, no change in total Smad2 was observed.
evidence: Stated in text describing western blot results, supported by Figure 6A.

claim: The level of phosphorylated p38 Mapk was significantly reduced in Rbfox2 mutant embryos.
source: Similarly, the level of phosphorylated p38 Mapk was significantly reduced, although there was no change in total p38 Mapk (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing reduced p-p38 Mapk levels (Figure 6A).

claim: No change in total p38 Mapk was observed in Rbfox2 mutant embryos.
source: Similarly, the level of phosphorylated p38 Mapk was significantly reduced, although there was no change in total p38 Mapk (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing similar total p38 Mapk levels (Figure 6A).

claim: Fn1 protein levels were significantly reduced in Rbfox2 mutant neural crest as compared with controls.
source: Consistent with the reduction in its mRNA levels, Fn1 protein levels were also significantly reduced in Rbfox2 mutant neural crest as compared with controls (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing reduced Fn1 protein levels (Figure 6B).

claim: Majority of the cultured palatal mesenchymal cells were GFP positive confirming their neural crest origin.
source: The neural crest cell's origin and purity were confirmed by growing cultures of Pax3Cre/+;Rbfox2flox/+;Rosa26mTmG/+ embryos. Majority of the cultured cells were GFP positive confirming their neural crest origin (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by fluorescent images showing GFP-positive cultured cells (Figure 6C).

claim: Palatal mesenchymal cells isolated from Rbfox2 mutant embryos showed reduced levels of both Tak1 and phosphorylated Tak1 when compared with control following TGF-β stimulation.
source: Consistent with the in vivo data, palatal mesenchymal cells isolated from Rbfox2 mutant embryos showed reduced levels of both Tak1 and phosphorylated Tak1 when compared with control following TGF-β stimulation (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data from TGF-β stimulated cultured cells (Figure 6D).

claim: No significant change in pTak1/Tak1 ratio was observed in Rbfox2 mutant cells, suggesting that Tak1 activation was not affected by Rbfox2 deletion.
source: In addition, no significant change in pTak1/Tak1 ratio was observed, suggesting that Tak1 activation was not affected by Rbfox2 deletion (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by quantification of western blot data showing similar pTak1/Tak1 ratio (Figure 6E).

claim: TGF-β-induced C-terminal Smad2 phosphorylation levels were reduced in Rbfox2 mutant cells when compared with controls.
source: Similarly, TGF-β-induced C-terminal Smad2 and p38 Mapk phosphorylation levels were reduced in Rbfox2 mutant cells when compared with controls, while no significant change was observed in total Smad2 or p38 Mapk (Figure 6D–E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by western blot data from TGF-β stimulated cultured cells (Figure 6D-E).

claim: TGF-β-induced p38 Mapk phosphorylation levels were reduced in Rbfox2 mutant cells when compared with controls.
source: Similarly, TGF-β-induced C-terminal Smad2 and p38 Mapk phosphorylation levels were reduced in Rbfox2 mutant cells when compared with controls, while no significant change was observed in total Smad2 or p38 Mapk (Figure 6D–E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by western blot data from TGF-β stimulated cultured cells (Figure 6D-E).

claim: No significant change was observed in total Smad2 in Rbfox2 mutant cells following TGF-β stimulation.
source: Similarly, TGF-β-induced C-terminal Smad2 and p38 Mapk phosphorylation levels were reduced in Rbfox2 mutant cells when compared with controls, while no significant change was observed in total Smad2 or p38 Mapk (Figure 6D–E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by western blot data from TGF-β stimulated cultured cells (Figure 6D-E).

claim: No significant change was observed in total p38 Mapk in Rbfox2 mutant cells following TGF-β stimulation.
source: Similarly, TGF-β-induced C-terminal Smad2 and p38 Mapk phosphorylation levels were reduced in Rbfox2 mutant cells when compared with controls, while no significant change was observed in total Smad2 or p38 Mapk (Figure 6D–E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by western blot data from TGF-β stimulated cultured cells (Figure 6D-E).

claim: Rbfox2-TGF-β-Tak1 signaling axis was impaired in Rbfox2 mutant cells.
source: Quantification of these proteins showed a significant reduction in the ratio of pSmad2-C/Smad2-C and p-p38 Mapk/p38 Mapk, suggesting that Rbfox2-TGF-β-Tak1 signaling axis was impaired in Rbfox2 mutant cells (Figure 6D–E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by quantification of western blot data showing reduced phosphorylation ratios (Figure 6D-E).

claim: Rbfox2 mutant palatal cells proliferate slower than control cells.
source: Consistent with the in vivo data, Rbfox2 mutant palatal cells proliferate slower than control cells and Tak1 overexpression can rescue the proliferation defects (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by Ki67 immunostaining and quantification data (Figure 6F-H).

claim: Tak1 overexpression can rescue the proliferation defects in Rbfox2 mutant palatal cells.
source: Consistent with the in vivo data, Rbfox2 mutant palatal cells proliferate slower than control cells and Tak1 overexpression can rescue the proliferation defects (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by Ki67 immunostaining and quantification data showing increased proliferation after Tak1 overexpression (Figure 6F-H).

claim: Both Tak1 and phosphorylated Tak1 levels were significantly increased after Tak1 transfection in Rbfox2 mutant cells.
source: We confirmed that both Tak1 and phosphorylated Tak1 levels were significantly increased after Tak1 transfection in Rbfox2 mutant cells (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing increased Tak1 and pTak1 after transfection (Figure 6G).

claim: Significant increase in the expression of Map3k7 and Fn1 was observed in Tak1 overexpressing Rbfox2 mutant cells.
source: Compared with empty vector transfected controls, we observed significant increase in the expression of Map3k7 and Fn1 in Tak1 overexpressing Rbfox2 mutant cells.
evidence: Stated in text describing qRT-PCR results, supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: No change in Myl1, Sfrs18 and Smarca2 expression was observed in Tak1 overexpressing Rbfox2 mutant cells.
source: No change in Myl1, Sfrs18 and Smarca2 expression was observed (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing no change in these genes (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).

claim: A significant increase in Rbfox2 expression was observed after TGF-β treatment in wildtype palatal mesenchymal cells.
source: To determine whether TGF-β signaling pathway regulate Rbfox2 expression in a positive feedback loop, we analyzed Rbfox2 expression in wildtype palatal mesenchymal cells after TGF-β stimulation. We observed a significant increase in Rbfox2 expression after TGF-β treatment (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing increased Rbfox2 expression after TGF-β stimulation (Figure 7A).

claim: Smad3 inhibitor abolished TGF-β-induced increase in Rbfox2 expression.
source: We observed that Smad3 inhibitor abolished TGF-β-induced increase in Rbfox2 expression (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing no Rbfox2 increase with Smad3 inhibitor (Figure 7B).

claim: A similar trend was observed with Tak1 inhibitor on TGF-β-induced Rbfox2 expression.
source: A similar trend was observed with Tak1 inhibitor (Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing reduced Rbfox2 increase with Tak1 inhibitor (Figure 7C).

claim: p38 inhibitor did not impact TGF-β-induced Rbfox2 expression.
source: However, p38 inhibitor did not impact TGF-β-induced Rbfox2 expression (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing no effect of p38 inhibitor on Rbfox2 expression (Figure 7D).

claim: TGF-β induces Rbfox2 expression either through Tak1-dependent or -independent canonical pathways.
source: Together, these results suggest that TGF-β induces Rbfox2 expression either through Tak1-dependent or -independent canonical pathways.
evidence: Inferred from inhibitor experiments showing Smad3 and Tak1 inhibitor effects but not p38 inhibitor effect (Figure 7B-D).

claim: Two sites with multiple Smad binding elements (SBEs) were identified in 2.5 kb Rbfox2 promoter.
source: To further investigate how Smad-dependent canonical pathway regulates Rbfox2 expression, we analyzed 2.5 kb Rbfox2 promoter and identified two sites with multiple Smad binding elements (SBEs).
evidence: Stated in text describing promoter analysis, supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Smad2, Smad3 or Smad4 significantly activated the Rbfox2 luciferase reporter in the presence/absence of recombinant TGF-β.
source: Smad2, Smad3 or Smad4 significantly activated the Rbfox2 luciferase reporter in the presence/absence of recombinant TGF-β.
evidence: Stated in text describing luciferase assay results, supported by Figure 7E-G.

claim: In the presence of recombinant TGF-β, the fold activation of Rbfox2 luciferase reporter by Smads was much higher when compared with no TGF-β stimulation.
source: However, in the presence of recombinant TGF-β, the fold activation was much higher when compared with no TGF-β stimulation (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data showing higher activation with TGF-β (Figure 7E-G).

claim: Smad2/3 binds directly to SBEs in the Rbfox2 promoter in vivo.
source: Using the wild-type palatal mesenchymal cells in the presence or absence of TGF-β, we next tested Smad2/3 binding activity to SBEs identified in the Rbfox2 promoter in vivo by chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assays. Our data indicate that Smad2/3 binds directly to these sites in vivo.
evidence: Supported by ChIP assay data showing Smad2/3 binding to Rbfox2 promoter (Figure 7H).

claim: Enrichment in Smad2/3 chromatin binding was observed after TGF-β treatment.
source: Moreover, we observed enrichment in Smad2/3 chromatin binding after TGF-β treatment (Figure 7H).
evidence: Supported by ChIP assay data showing increased Smad2/3 binding after TGF-β treatment (Figure 7H).

claim: Rbfox2 expression in neural crest-derived palatal mesenchymal cells is tightly regulated by TGF-β signaling pathway.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that Rbfox2 expression in neural crest-derived palatal mesenchymal cells is tightly regulated by TGF-β signaling pathway (Figure 7I).
evidence: Supported by multiple experiments showing TGF-β regulation of Rbfox2 expression (Figure 7A-H).

claim: Approximately 3–4% of infants are born with congenital diseases.
source: Approximately 3–4% of infants are born with congenital diseases.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Craniofacial and cardiovascular abnormalities are the most common defects, contributing to more than one-third of the congenital diseases.
source: Collectively, craniofacial and cardiovascular abnormalities are the most common defects, contributing to more than one-third of the congenital diseases.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: NCCs are a transient population of migratory progenitor cells that reside in the dorsal side of the neural tube.
source: NCCs are a transient population of migratory progenitor cells that reside in the dorsal side of the neural tube.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: NCCs can be subdivided into five axial populations: cranial, cardiac, vagal, trunk and sacral NC cells.
source: NCCs can be subdivided into five axial populations: cranial, cardiac, vagal, trunk and sacral NC cells.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Lineage-tracing experiments in mouse embryos have demonstrated that NCCs differentiate into a diverse array of cell types including the craniofacial skeletal elements, autonomous nervous system of the heart and GI-tract, as well as smooth muscle cells of the cardiac OFT.
source: Lineage-tracing experiments in mouse embryos have demonstrated that NCCs differentiate into a diverse array of cell types including the craniofacial skeletal elements, autonomous nervous system of the heart and GI-tract, as well as smooth muscle cells of the cardiac OFT (Chai et al., 2000; Jiang et al., 2002; Jiang et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2004; Martik and Bronner, 2017; Plein et al., 2015; Waldo et al., 1999; Yoshida et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous lineage-tracing studies.

claim: Cranial NCCs migrate from anterior portions of the folded neural tube and contribute to the formation of the skull, cartilage, and connective tissue.
source: Cranial NCCs migrate from anterior portions of the folded neural tube and contribute to the formation of the skull, cartilage, and connective tissue, where they populate the first and second pharyngeal arches that give rise to cranial ganglia, the maxilla, the mandible, palates and other structures of the developing head (Chai et al., 2000; Jiang et al., 2002; Martik and Bronner, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on cranial NCC development.

claim: In mammals, both the primary and secondary palates are morphologically visible as early as E11.5.
source: In mammals, both the primary and secondary palates are morphologically visible as early as E11.5 as demonstrated by an outgrowth from the oral side of the medial nasal and maxillary processes, respectively.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about palate development.

claim: The primary palate is formed by fusion of the maxillary prominence with the frontonasal prominence.
source: The primary palate is formed by fusion of the maxillary prominence with the frontonasal prominence (Bush and Jiang, 2012; Dixon et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on palate development.

claim: Secondary palates are formed from the outgrowths of neural crest-derived mesenchyme that lie on either side of the developing tongue.
source: Secondary palates are formed from the outgrowths of neural crest-derived mesenchyme that lie on either side of the developing tongue (Bush and Jiang, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on palate development.

claim: Palatal shelves elevate between E13.5 and E14.5 to a horizontal position above the tongue, grow toward the midline and fuse with each other to form an intact palate.
source: Initially, palatal shelves grow vertically flanking the developing tongue, but they elevate between E13.5 and E14.5 to a horizontal position above the tongue, grow toward the midline and fuse with each other to form an intact palate (Bush and Jiang, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on palate development.

claim: Functional defects in NCCs result in craniofacial malformations including cleft lip and/or cleft palate.
source: Functional defects in NCCs result in craniofacial malformations including cleft lip and/or cleft palate.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about NCC function.

claim: Many transcription factors, chromatin remodeling factors, non-coding RNA and signaling molecules have been implicated in impaired neural crest development that result in cardio-craniofacial syndromes.
source: Many transcription factors, chromatin remodeling factors, non-coding RNA and signaling molecules have been implicated in impaired neural crest development that result in cardio-craniofacial syndromes (Bélanger et al., 2018; Martik and Bronner, 2017; Plein et al., 2015; Singh et al., 2013; Strobl-Mazzulla et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on neural crest development.

claim: The cell-autonomous role of splicing regulators in neural crest biology remains unclear and warrants further investigation.
source: However, the cell-autonomous role of splicing regulators in neural crest biology remains unclear and warrants further investigation.
evidence: Stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: AS of pre-messenger RNAs is essential for regulating gene expression and creating proteomic diversity.
source: AS of pre-messenger RNAs is essential for regulating gene expression and creating proteomic diversity.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about alternative splicing.

claim: Changes in exon inclusion or exclusion can produce multiple mRNAs and protein isoforms with related or distinct functions.
source: Changes in exon inclusion or exclusion can produce multiple mRNAs and protein isoforms with related or distinct functions.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about alternative splicing.

claim: The RNA-binding fox-1 (Rbfox) homolog proteins: Rbfox1, Rbfox2, and Rbfox3 are evolutionarily conserved splicing factors.
source: The RNA-binding fox-1 (Rbfox) homolog proteins: Rbfox1, Rbfox2, and Rbfox3 are evolutionarily conserved splicing factors that have been implicated in diverse cellular processes such as cell proliferation, cell death and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (Kuroyanagi, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on Rbfox proteins.

claim: A conserved RNA-Recognition Motif that recognizes UGCAUG element in the introns, flanking target exons, characterizes Rbfox proteins.
source: A conserved RNA-Recognition Motif that recognizes UGCAUG element in the introns, flanking target exons, characterizes Rbfox proteins (Jin et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on Rbfox proteins.

claim: Rbfox proteins regulate splicing either positively or negatively, depending on their binding sites.
source: Rbfox proteins regulate splicing either positively or negatively, depending on their binding sites.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about Rbfox protein function.

claim: Rbfox proteins promote exon skipping or inclusion when they bind to either the upstream or downstream of the alternative exon.
source: They promote exon skipping or inclusion when they bind to either the upstream or downstream of the alternative exon (Jin et al., 2003; Ponthier et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on Rbfox protein function.

claim: In addition to splicing, Rbfox proteins also regulate transcriptional gene networks.
source: In addition to splicing, Rbfox proteins also regulate transcriptional gene networks (Fogel et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on Rbfox protein function.

claim: All Rbfox proteins bind to the same recognition sequence, but their in vivo functions are only partially redundant due to their markedly distinct expression pattern.
source: Although all Rbfox proteins bind to the same recognition sequence, their in vivo functions are only partially redundant due to their markedly distinct expression pattern.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about Rbfox protein function.

claim: Both Rbfox1 (A2BP1) and Rbfox2 (RBM9) are expressed in the neurons, heart and skeletal muscle.
source: Both Rbfox1 (A2BP1) and Rbfox2 (RBM9) are expressed in the neurons, heart and skeletal muscle (Gehman et al., 2012; Gehman et al., 2011; Singh et al., 2014; Wei et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on Rbfox expression patterns.

claim: Rbfox3 (NeuN or HRNBP3) expression is more restricted to neuronal tissues.
source: Unlike the aforementioned, Rbfox3 (NeuN or HRNBP3) expression is more restricted to neuronal tissues (Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on Rbfox3 expression.

claim: Several diseases have been associated with dysregulation of splicing.
source: Several diseases have been associated with dysregulation of splicing (Garcia-Blanco et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous review on splicing and disease.

claim: Genetic deletion of Rbfox1 and Rbfox2 in the nervous system increased susceptibility to seizures and impaired cerebellum development, respectively.
source: For example, genetic deletion of Rbfox1 and Rbfox2 in the nervous system increased susceptibility to seizures and impaired cerebellum development, respectively (Gehman et al., 2012; Gehman et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on Rbfox function in nervous system.

claim: Morpholino-mediated knockdown of Rbfox1 and Rbfox2 in zebrafish embryos impaired cardiac and skeletal muscle functions.
source: Morpholino-mediated knockdown of Rbfox1 and Rbfox2 in zebrafish embryos impaired cardiac and skeletal muscle functions (Gallagher et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on Rbfox function in zebrafish.

claim: During skeletal muscle development, Rbfox2-mediated splicing is required for myoblast fusion and differentiation.
source: During skeletal muscle development, Rbfox2-mediated splicing is required for myoblast fusion and differentiation (Runfola et al., 2015; Singh et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on Rbfox2 function in skeletal muscle.

claim: Decreased Rbfox2 expression has been reported in response to transverse aortic constriction in the mouse heart.
source: Decreased Rbfox2 expression has been reported in response to transverse aortic constriction in the mouse heart, and cardiac-specific deletion leads to pressure overload-induced heart failure (Wei et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on Rbfox2 function in heart.

claim: Cardiac-specific deletion of Rbfox2 leads to pressure overload-induced heart failure.
source: Decreased Rbfox2 expression has been reported in response to transverse aortic constriction in the mouse heart, and cardiac-specific deletion leads to pressure overload-induced heart failure (Wei et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on Rbfox2 function in heart.

claim: Abnormal expression of Rbfox2 has been associated with hypoplastic left heart syndrome.
source: Abnormal expression of Rbfox2 has also been associated with hypoplastic left heart syndrome (Verma et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on Rbfox2 and heart disease.

claim: Elevated Rbfox2 protein expression in diabetic hearts affects diabetes-induced AS of cardiac-specific genes.
source: Recently, Nutter et al. (2016) demonstrated that elevated Rbfox2 protein expression in diabetic hearts affects diabetes-induced AS of cardiac-specific genes.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on Rbfox2 in diabetic hearts.

claim: The cell-autonomous role of Rbfox2 in the functioning of neural crest cells has not been explored.
source: Despite extensive studies of Rbfox2 regulation on neuronal, cardiac and skeletal muscle cells, the cell-autonomous role of Rbfox2 in the functioning of neural crest cells has not been explored.
evidence: Stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: Neural crest-specific deletion of Tak1 results in the cleft palate.
source: Map3k7 encodes transforming growth factor β (TGF-β)-activated kinase 1 (Tak1) required for the proliferation of palatal mesenchymal cells. Neural crest-specific deletion of Tak1 results in the cleft palate (Song et al., 2013; Yumoto et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on Tak1 function in palate development.

claim: Neural crest-specific deletion of Fn1 leads to the cleft palate development.
source: Fibronectin 1 (Fn1), which is a component of the extracellular matrix, has various alternatively spliced variants. Wang et al. recently demonstrated that neural crest-specific deletion of Fn1 leads to the cleft palate development (Wang and Astrof, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on Fn1 function in palate development.

claim: Rbfox2 can affect transcript stability by directly binding to the 3'UTR of target genes.
source: For example, Rbfox2 can affect transcript stability by directly binding to the 3'UTR of target genes (Damianov et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on Rbfox2 function.

claim: Rbfox2 may affect gene expression by recruiting polycomb complexes to the DNA.
source: Rbfox2 may affect gene expression by recruiting polycomb complexes to the DNA (Wei et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on Rbfox2 function.

claim: The importance of both canonical and non-canonical TGF-β signaling pathways in craniofacial development, including secondary palate formation, has been studied extensively.
source: The importance of both canonical and non-canonical TGF-β signaling pathways in craniofacial development, including secondary palate formation, has been studied extensively (Iwata et al., 2012; Massagué, 2012; Shim et al., 2009; Song et al., 2013; Yumoto et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on TGF-β signaling in craniofacial development.

claim: Canonical TGF-β signaling occurs via activation of receptor-regulated Smads (R-Smads) 2/3.
source: Canonical TGF-β signaling occurs via activation of receptor-regulated Smads (R-Smads) 2/3.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about TGF-β signaling.

claim: Non-canonical TGF-β signaling occurs via activation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, including TGF-β-activated kinase 1 (Tak1).
source: However, non-canonical TGF-β signaling occurs via activation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, including TGF-β-activated kinase 1 (Tak1) (Massagué, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous review on TGF-β signaling.

claim: TGF-β signaling is required in the NCCs to regulate cell proliferation during palatogenesis.
source: TGF-β signaling is required in the NCCs to regulate cell proliferation during palatogenesis (Iwata et al., 2012; Song et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on TGF-β signaling in palate development.

claim: In humans, altered TGF-β signaling pathway has been associated with both syndromic and non-syndromic cleft palates.
source: In humans, altered TGF-β signaling pathway has been associated with both syndromic and non-syndromic cleft palates.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about TGF-β signaling and human disease.

claim: Mutations in either TGF-β receptor type I (TGFBR1) or type II (TGFBR2) are associated with Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
source: For instance, mutations in either TGF-β receptor type I (TGFBR1) or type II (TGFBR2) are associated with Loeys-Dietz syndrome (Loeys et al., 2005; Mizuguchi et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on Loeys-Dietz syndrome.

claim: Patients with Loeys-Dietz syndrome have craniofacial malformations, including cleft palate, craniosynostosis and hypertelorism.
source: Patients with Loeys-Dietz syndrome have craniofacial malformations, including cleft palate, craniosynostosis and hypertelorism (Loeys et al., 2005; Mizuguchi et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on Loeys-Dietz syndrome.

claim: Patients with Marfan or DiGeorge syndrome develop craniofacial malformations from altered TGF-β signaling.
source: Similarly, patients with Marfan or DiGeorge syndrome develop craniofacial malformations from altered TGF-β signaling (Brooke et al., 2008; Kalluri and Han, 2008; Lindsay, 2001; Wurdak et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on Marfan and DiGeorge syndromes.

claim: Neural crest-specific genetic inactivation of several TGF-β receptors in mice, including BmprIa, Tgfbr1, and Tgfbr2 causes craniofacial deformities, including cleft palate.
source: In mice, neural crest-specific genetic inactivation of several TGF-β receptors in mice, including BmprIa, Tgfbr1, and Tgfbr2 causes craniofacial deformities, including cleft palate (Dudas et al., 2006; Ito et al., 2003; Li et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on TGF-β receptors in mouse craniofacial development.

claim: Tak1 is required in the NCCs to activate both TGF-β-induced canonical (R-Smads) and non-canonical (p38 Mapk) pathways.
source: Recent studies in mice demonstrated that Tak1 is required in the NCCs to activate both TGF-β-induced canonical (R-Smads) and non-canonical (p38 Mapk) pathways (Yumoto et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on Tak1 function in NCCs.

claim: Fn1 and its integrin receptor positively regulate TGF-β signaling by promoting the receptor complex formation on the cell surface.
source: Fn1 and its integrin receptor positively regulate TGF-β signaling by promoting the receptor complex formation on the cell surface (Tian et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on Fn1 function.

claim: Fibronectin regulates TGF-β by controlling the matrix assembly of latent TGF-β-binding protein-1.
source: Fibronectin also regulates TGF-β by controlling the matrix assembly of latent TGF-β-binding protein-1 (Dallas et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on fibronectin function.

claim: TGF-β1 induces Fn1 expression via a Smad independent pathway.
source: In a reciprocal manner, TGF-β1 induces Fn1 expression via a Smad independent pathway (Hocevar et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on TGF-β1 regulation of Fn1.

claim: Meg3 modulates the expression of TGF-β pathway genes by binding to the distal regulatory elements.
source: Meg3 modulates the expression of TGF-β pathway genes by binding to the distal regulatory elements (Mondal et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on Meg3 function.

claim: Chondrocyte-specific deletion of Tak1 results in severe chondrodysplasia with impaired ossification and joint abnormalities including tarsal fusion.
source: Chondrocyte-specific deletion of Tak1 results in severe chondrodysplasia with impaired ossification and joint abnormalities including tarsal fusion (Shim et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on Tak1 function in chondrocytes.

claim: Osteoblast-specific deletion of Tak1 results in clavicular hypoplasia and delayed fontanelle fusion.
source: Osteoblast-specific deletion of Tak1 results in clavicular hypoplasia and delayed fontanelle fusion (Greenblatt et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on Tak1 function in osteoblasts.

claim: The striking similarities in craniofacial and skeletal phenotypes between Tak1 and Rbfox2 mutants suggest that Tak1 is a downstream target of Rbfox2.
source: Altogether, the striking similarities in craniofacial and skeletal phenotypes between Tak1 and Rbfox2 mutants suggest that Tak1 is a downstream target of Rbfox2 and it may significantly contribute to the phenotype observed in Rbfox2 mutant embryos.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of phenotypes between Tak1 and Rbfox2 mutants.

claim: Tak1 may significantly contribute to the phenotype observed in Rbfox2 mutant embryos.
source: Altogether, the striking similarities in craniofacial and skeletal phenotypes between Tak1 and Rbfox2 mutants suggest that Tak1 is a downstream target of Rbfox2 and it may significantly contribute to the phenotype observed in Rbfox2 mutant embryos.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of phenotypes and rescue experiments.

claim: Tak1 regulates neural crest-derived tissues downstream of Rbfox2.
source: Furthermore, restoration of TGF-β signaling by Tak1 overexpression can rescue the proliferation defects seen in Rbfox2 mutant embryos. This indicates that Tak1 regulates neural crest-derived tissues downstream of Rbfox2.
evidence: Inferred from Tak1 rescue experiments showing restoration of proliferation in Rbfox2 mutants.

claim: Other Rbfox2 target genes identified in the RNA-Seq screen may be responsible or contribute to the craniofacial phenotype present in Rbfox2 mutant embryos.
source: It is possible that other Rbfox2 target genes identified in our RNA-Seq screen may be responsible or contribute to the craniofacial phenotype present in Rbfox2 mutant embryos.
evidence: Stated as speculation about potential contributions of other target genes.

claim: Changes in the expression levels of splicing factors must be tightly regulated during embryonic development.
source: Since a single splicing factor affects the expression/splicing of numerous genes and displays profound downstream effects, changes in the expression levels of splicing factors must be tightly regulated during embryonic development (Baralle and Giudice, 2017; Revil et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous reviews on splicing regulation and inferred from the broad effects of splicing factors.

claim: Altered TGF-β signaling is well studied in multiple human congenital malformations and syndromes.
source: Given that altered TGF-β signaling is well studied in multiple human congenital malformations and syndromes, our observation may be relevant in human disease studies.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about TGF-β signaling in human disease.

claim: The observation of Rbfox2-TGF-β-Tak1 signaling axis may be relevant in human disease studies.
source: Given that altered TGF-β signaling is well studied in multiple human congenital malformations and syndromes, our observation may be relevant in human disease studies.
evidence: Stated as speculation about potential relevance to human disease.
